key_insight: CKD detection accuracy fell from 83.9% to 61.5% when SMOTE was confined to training data, highlighting how preprocessing can inflate reported performance.
clinical_relevance: Widely available full blood counts may offer a low-cost signal for CKD, but these results do not establish a reliable clinical screening tool.
method: Used age, cardiovascular disease and eight full blood count parameters from 155 Ghanaian hospital patients.
Compared 11 algorithms, six resampling strategies and 13 ensembles using repeated stratified cross-validation.
Contrasted SMOTE before splitting with resampling restricted to training folds.
evidence_signal: Among 155 patients, 43 had CKD; training-only resampling yielded 61.5% accuracy and an AUC of 0.604 in 39 held-out patients.
watch_item: The deployed models used pre-split SMOTE, risking data leakage and inflated performance; independent validation is needed before clinical use.
paper_title: Machine Learning Based Detection of Chronic Kidney Disease using Full Blood Count from a Ghanaian Hospital Population with an Integrated Web Application
